tagline: A mountainside road shortened the journey between Newburgh and West Point.
intro: Storm King Highway winds along the steep slopes above the Hudson, reaching 420 feet above the water. This two-lane section of NY 218 has a rubblestone wall on its river side and grades no steeper than 7 percent. Its civil engineering earned National Register recognition in 1982.

Local business and community groups pressed for a connection through the Highlands; highway commissioner Gordon Reel took up the idea in 1913. Surveyors sometimes rappelled down cliffs to mark the route before construction began in 1916. A proposed tunnel gave way to an open cut because lighting would cost too much and the tunnel would miss the scenery. The 1922 opening cut 22 miles from the automobile journey between Newburgh and West Point. The first contractor went bankrupt, and its replacement faced a labor shortage when the United States entered World War I. The Palisades Interstate Park Commission renegotiated the contract to account for those wartime difficulties. In 1940, four-lane US 9W west of Storm King shortened the journey further.

Traveling south from Cornwall-on-Hudson, the historic section runs to Lee Road in the Town of Highlands. Small pullouts offer views of the Hudson and mountains including Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill. Highland Falls lies beside the United States Military Academy at West Point.
notice: A rubblestone wall follows the river side of the highway.

moments.title: Camp Olmsted
moments.text: Camp Olmsted occupies land on Bayview Avenue, NY 218, near Storm King Mountain. The Methodist Five Points Mission founded the camp in 1901 for children of immigrant families it helped in Manhattan. The camp began with a parcel of 21 acres donated by Sarah and John Olmsted, under the name Olmsted Fresh Air Home. Campers traveled from the city to Cornwall aboard the Hudson River Day Liner. Winterizing three cabins allowed year-round operation in 1966; the camp continues to serve city children in summer and host religious retreats throughout the year.

moments.title: Storm King Highway pullouts
moments.text: The pullouts give views across the Hudson toward Breakneck Ridge and Bull Hill. Building this road meant working above another transport route: the New York Central Railroad’s West Shore Line. Dislodged boulders sometimes blocked its tracks or damaged rail cars and their contents. The mountain remains a source of hazards, including rockfall and falling ice. In July 2023, a flash flood washed out both lanes and the retaining wall along an entire section of highway. A rubblestone wall borders the river side of the road, and chainlink gates stand at both ends.

moments.title: Highland Falls Village Hall
moments.text: Round brick arches frame the upper windows of Highland Falls Village Hall, a three-story brick building on Main Street. The local tax assessor dates the building to 1894, though its exact construction year and original purpose are unknown. First National Bank acquired it in 1907, when storefronts were added and the southernmost upper windows were bricked in. The village bought the property in 1967 and has used it without significant alterations since. Glass storefronts remain at street level, north of the central entrance with its round arch and fluted pilasters.

practical: Storm King Highway pullouts: The Department of Transportation closes the road during heavy rain or snow because of rockfall, avalanche and falling-ice hazards. (checked 2026-10-11)
